faq.q: Why does hyponatremia cause brain swelling?

exam: A patient with malaria presents with confusion and serum Na⁺ 118 mmol/L — what is the immediate management and why? — Stop rapid free‑water infusion, give hypertonic saline cautiously, monitor neurologic status.
You have a child with severe vomiting, Na⁺ 150 mmol/L, no labs for osmolality — how do you estimate safe correction? — Use the 10 mmol/L/24 h rule, give hypotonic fluids slowly, watch for seizures.
Explain why ADH antagonists are contraindicated in acute hyponatremia — they block water reabsorption, risking further rapid drop in serum sodium and worsening cerebral edema.

A trauma patient loses both blood and water, serum Na⁺ 135 mmol/L, but shows peripheral edema — what does this tell you about ICF? — ECF loss with relative ICF expansion; give isotonic crystalloids first.

How does severe burns affect intracellular fluid volume? — Capillary leak shifts protein‑rich fluid to interstitium, reducing oncotic pressure and pulling water out of cells; aggressive albumin and careful fluid replacement are needed.
Distinguish cerebral edema from cerebral dehydration on exam — cerebral edema presents with papilledema, decreased consciousness; dehydration shows dry mucosa, sunken eyes, normal fundi.
Why is rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia dangerous? — It creates an osmotic gradient that pulls water out of brain cells, causing demyelination.
In a low‑resource setting without serum osmolality, how can you suspect hyperosmolar ICF loss? — Look for signs of dehydration, high urine specific gravity, and hypernatremia on basic chemistry.
ai.title: Intracellular Fluid Physiology
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Intracellular fluid (ICF) makes up about two‑thirds of total body water and is essential for cellular function. Its volume is tightly regulated by osmotic gradients and membrane pumps, and disturbances can cause life‑threatening electrolyte shifts.

b: Separated from extracellular fluid (ECF) by the phospholipid bilayer
Contains high K⁺, low Na⁺, and high protein concentration
sections.p: ICF is the water contained within all cells, roughly 28 L in a 70‑kg adult (≈40 % of body weight, 2/3 of total body water). It provides the medium for metabolic reactions and maintains cell shape.

b: Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase pumps 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, consuming ATP
Aquaporins allow rapid water movement following osmotic gradients
sections.p: Cell membranes use Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase, aquaporins, and ion channels to keep ICF volume stable. Osmotic equilibrium between ICF and ECF is achieved when the sum of solutes (osmoles) is equal on both sides.

b: ADH increases water reabsorption → lowers plasma osmolarity → water shifts into cells
Aldosterone promotes Na⁺ retention → expands ECF, pulling water out of cells
sections.p: Hormonal and neural mechanisms adjust ICF volume indirectly by altering ECF osmolarity and total body water.

b: Hypernatremia → extracellular hyperosmolarity → ICF loss → neuronal shrinkage, seizures
Hyponatremia → extracellular hypoosmolarity → ICF gain → cerebral edema, coma
Cell membrane injury (e.g., severe malaria, bacterial toxins) → loss of Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase → intracellular edema
sections.p: Disruption of osmotic balance or membrane pumps leads to cellular swelling or shrinkage, impairing organ function.

b: Rapid correction of severe hyponatremia risks osmotic demyelination
Gradual correction of hypernatremia avoids cerebral hemorrhage
sections.p: Recognising ICF disturbances guides fluid therapy, electrolyte correction, and monitoring in critically ill patients, especially where labs are limited.

t.b: Is the extracellular osmolarity abnormal? – Low Na⁺ indicates risk of ICF overload; high Na⁺ indicates ICF depletion
Confirms true hypo‑ or hyper‑osmolar state – guides rate of correction
Helps differentiate renal vs extrarenal causes of sodium imbalance

b: Always assess mental status – early sign of cerebral edema or shrinkage
Calculate correction rate: hyponatremia ≤ 8 mmol/L/24 h, hypernatremia ≤ 10 mmol/L/24 h
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to link fluid shifts to clinical signs, choose safe correction strategies, and recognise when ICF changes are life‑threatening.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe neurological deterioration (coma, seizures) with abnormal sodium
Rapidly rising serum sodium > 160 mmol/L or falling < 115 mmol/L
